Some of her hits include "Who's Sorry Now," which reached #4 in the US and #1 in the UK, and "Stupid Cupid," which hit #14 in the US and #1 in the UK as well. I think "Fallin'" peaked around #30 in the US and possibly #17 in the UK, but I should clarify that it’s not the same song as Alicia Keys’ "Fallin'." “**Fallin’**” is a late-1950s pop/rock-and-roll song recorded by **Connie Francis** during the early breakout phase of her career.

## Basic facts

- **Artist:** Connie Francis  
- **Title:** “Fallin’”  
- **Songwriters:** **Neil Sedaka** and **Howard Greenfield**  
- **Released:** 1958  
- **Label:** MGM Records  
- **Genre/style:** Teen pop, early rock-and-roll-influenced pop  
- **Era:** Issued soon after Francis’s breakthrough with “Who’s Sorry Now?” and around the same period as “Stupid Cupid”  
- **Chart performance:** It became a moderate hit, reaching the U.S. pop charts; it is generally cited as peaking around **No. 30 on the Billboard Hot 100**.

## Background

“Fallin’” came from the songwriting team of **Neil Sedaka and Howard Greenfield**, who were part of the Brill Building/Aldon Music pop-writing world that helped shape late-1950s and early-1960s teen pop. Sedaka and Greenfield also wrote **“Stupid Cupid,”** one of Connie Francis’s best-known early rock-and-roll hits.

Connie Francis had first become a major star in 1958 with **“Who’s Sorry Now?”**, a revival of an older standard. After that success, MGM and Francis began looking for material that could appeal to the rapidly expanding teenage record-buying audience. Songs like “Stupid Cupid” and “Fallin’” moved her image somewhat away from traditional ballads and toward contemporary youth pop.

## Musical style

“Fallin’” is an upbeat, lightly rocking pop number rather than a dramatic ballad. It has the brisk, catchy style associated with Sedaka and Greenfield’s early writing:

- energetic teen-pop rhythm  
- melodic, hook-driven chorus  
- lyrics about the rush and vulnerability of falling in love  
- a polished studio-pop arrangement typical of MGM’s late-1950s productions

It is not as hard-driving as some rock-and-roll records of the period, but it clearly reflects the pop-rock crossover sound that helped Francis connect with younger listeners.

## Place in Connie Francis’s career

“Fallin’” belongs to the first major wave of Connie Francis hits, alongside:

- “Who’s Sorry Now?”  
- “I’m Sorry I Made You Cry”  
- “Stupid Cupid”  
- “My Happiness”  
- “Among My Souvenirs”

While it was not one of her biggest signature records, it helped maintain her chart momentum in 1958 and demonstrated her versatility. Francis could sing standards, torch songs, novelty tunes, country-tinged pop, Italian-language material, and teenage rock-and-roll-styled songs.

## Connection to Neil Sedaka and Howard Greenfield

The song is notable partly because of the Sedaka-Greenfield connection. Neil Sedaka would soon become a major recording star himself with hits such as:

- “The Diary”  
- “Oh! Carol”  
- “Calendar Girl”  
- “Breaking Up Is Hard to Do”

Howard Greenfield was one of Sedaka’s most important lyric-writing partners. Their work for Connie Francis helped establish them as successful pop songwriters before Sedaka’s own performing career fully took off.

## Not to be confused with other songs

Connie Francis’s “Fallin’” is unrelated to:

- **“Fallin’” by Alicia Keys**  
- **“Falling” by Harry Styles**  
- other songs with similar titles such as “Falling in Love Again” or “Can’t Help Falling in Love”

The Connie Francis song is a distinct 1958 teen-pop recording.

## Availability

“Fallin’” has appeared on various Connie Francis compilations, especially collections focused on her early MGM singles or complete hit recordings. It is usually found on anthology releases rather than being remembered as one of her very biggest standalone classics.

## Summary

“**Fallin’**” is a 1958 Connie Francis single written by **Neil Sedaka and Howard Greenfield**. It is a catchy early teen-pop/rock-and-roll-influenced recording from the period when Francis was transitioning from revival ballads into contemporary youth-oriented pop. Though not as famous as “Who’s Sorry Now?” or “Stupid Cupid,” it was a charting hit and remains an important part of her early career and her association with the Sedaka-Greenfield songwriting team.
